title: Learning piano from his mother and uncle
summary: His mother taught him notes on the family upright, and his vaudeville uncle encouraged him; music was all he wanted.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Is that why you decided to take the piano? Or was it any conscious thought you were on?

I had no reason, John. John, I had no other reason but that I just loved this sound and I wanted to do it. I don't know. I can't say that I wanted to do it to prove anything. I just wanted to play it. And my mother had a piano. She had one of these old upright pianos.

Right in your house. Yeah, right in the house. And she played a little bit. Not very well. She would have loved to play. But she played a very bad bass. She played a good treble. But the bass, oh, she used the same bass for every key, you know. But Lord, she really gave me a good start and she showed me the notes, you know. And it really gave me, I guess, the incentive that I needed.
I see. Did she play any particular kind of piano or just a...

No, she could just play the waltzes and read a little bit, you know. And she played a little... She could just stumble through things to a grade. She only took about three or four months of lessons, you know.
Did you have a formal teacher that taught you?

Well, I started off, like I say, with my mother. And, of course, my uncle, Dui Shmead, who was known as Wilbur Leroy, and show business, he was a vaudeville, I can't. He played a little fake piano, you know. And he used to always encourage me, you know, and show me little tricks and chords and things that he used to know. And, of course, I know that all of this was a great incentive for me, but somehow or another, I don't know how to explain this, but I just didn't know anything else. It's the only thing I knew. I had no desire to become a doctor, a lawyer, an architect, an engineer, not even to be a millionaire. I wasn't even thinking of money. Like today, everybody thinks of how much they're going to make, you know. I mean, when I was playing, I wasn't thinking of how much I was going to make, or whether I was going to be able to make enough to retire the first five years I was playing or the first ten years. All I wanted to do was to play that piano and say I could play it. Not to say, not to have the satisfaction of saying I could play it, but because I really wanted to play it. This is the one thing I want to do. And I never missed an opportunity to pick up anything that I've heard. Of course, you never had the advantages that you have today. You know, I mean, radio was at a minimum, and you had very little records that you could listen to, and no sound equipment or anything. But, of course, you had the old player pianos, you know, that you could listen to.
